topics.question: What is a dataset's unit of observation and why does it matter?
topics.coverage: Compare people, visits and households; show how counting repeated visits as independent people changes a result.

topics.question: Why can the average hide the experience of most people?
topics.coverage: Compare mean, median, spread and skew using a labeled income-like distribution without implying it represents actual incomes.

topics.question: How can a survey miss people even when it receives thousands of answers?
topics.coverage: Trace sampling frames, recruitment, nonresponse and weighting; distinguish sample size from representativeness.

topics.question: What changes when a measurement is rounded before analysis?
topics.coverage: Use repeated sensor values to show resolution, uncertainty and accumulated rounding effects.

topics.question: What does a confidence interval say about a method rather than one fixed parameter?
topics.coverage: Use repeated simulated samples and state the sampling assumptions; distinguish frequentist coverage from posterior probability.

topics.question: Why does a small p-value fail to tell us whether an effect is important?
topics.coverage: Separate null model, sample size, effect size and practical relevance with an illustrative experiment.

topics.question: How can a correlation reverse when groups are combined?
topics.coverage: Work through a small table with different group sizes; identify the causal question before choosing an adjustment.

topics.question: Why can testing many hypotheses produce impressive-looking false discoveries?
topics.coverage: Compare preplanned tests, exploratory searching and multiplicity; avoid treating an adjustment as a guarantee of truth.

topics.question: What makes a model good at prediction but poor at explaining causes?
topics.coverage: Contrast held-out accuracy, interventions, confounding and transport to new populations.

topics.question: How can missing data change an analysis even after incomplete rows are removed?
topics.coverage: Compare missingness mechanisms and sensitivity checks; avoid claiming imputation reconstructs unknowable values.

topics.question: Why can an accurate classifier fail a rare-event screening task?
topics.coverage: Use a confusion matrix with explicit prevalence; compare precision, sensitivity, calibration and consequences.

topics.question: What does a reproducible analysis need beyond publishing its final chart?
topics.coverage: Trace raw data permissions, cleaning decisions, code, environment and uncertainty; keep personal records protected.

topics.question: How can a chart make equal changes look unequal?
topics.coverage: Compare truncated axes, log scales, binning and denominators using the same data.

topics.question: How do Bayesian and frequentist analyses ask different questions about the same unknown quantity?
topics.coverage: Work through one labeled estimation example, separating likelihood, prior, estimator, interval and uncertainty interpretation; do not imply the two frameworks are interchangeable or that one always wins.

topics.question: How can a chart show uncertainty without making every outcome look equally likely?
topics.coverage: Compare interval bars, distributions, sample variation and conditional scenarios using the same illustrative data; distinguish measurement uncertainty from modeled future variation.

topics.question: How can a dataset value change between an instrument reading and a published table?
topics.coverage: Trace calibration, units, transcription, cleaning, aggregation and version records through one fictional measurement; distinguish provenance from merely naming a storage platform.

topics.question: How can a predictive feature accidentally contain information from after the event being predicted?
topics.coverage: Trace timestamps, preprocessing, target construction and train-test separation in a harmless synthetic dataset; distinguish leakage from ordinary overfitting or a distribution shift.

topics.question: What did Berkeley?s fall 1973 graduate admissions data show before and after department adjustment?
topics.coverage: Use Bickel, Hammel and O?Connell?s published admissions tables for the 1973 cycle to compare campus totals with department-stratified results; distinguish statistical association, application patterns and any causal claim of discrimination.

topics.question: How did the 2020 U.S. Census Disclosure Avoidance System trade tabular precision for formal privacy protection?
topics.coverage: Trace the Census Bureau?s published TopDown disclosure-avoidance design and one 2020 redistricting data product; identify noisy tabulations, protected records, invariant totals and the accuracy/privacy tradeoff without claiming that all outputs or uses have identical error.

topics.question: What did the American Statistical Association?s 2016 p-value statement actually warn researchers against?
topics.coverage: Read the six principles in the dated ASA statement and compare threshold-only decisions with effect size, design, model assumptions and transparent reporting; separate the association?s statement from later editorial or task-force positions.

topics.question: How did Wells Fargo?s cross-selling targets distort an account-count performance measure?
topics.coverage: Use the CFPB?s 2016 consent order to trace the stated sales incentives and unauthorized account practices as an incentive-gaming case; distinguish enforcement findings from a universal statistical law or an estimate of every affected account.

# Statistics & Data Channel Master Topic Roadmap (Scratch to Advanced)
**Niche:** 121 Statistics & Data (Math_Scientific_Methods)  
**Channel Language:** English (YouTube)  
**Target Audience:** Data Scientists, Statisticians, Analysts, Machine Learning Engineers, Curious Decision-Makers (Global)  
**Production Format:** 10-Minute Documentary Explainer Episodes (600s, 75 Fixed 8s Scenes)  
**Execution & Sync Report:** [topics/121_statistics_data/TOPICS_COVERED_REPORT.md](./TOPICS_COVERED_REPORT.md)

## 1. Channel Progression Strategy

This curriculum organizes the core disciplines of Statistics & Data across four progressive tiers:
- **Tier 1: Descriptive Statistics, Probability Foundations & Distributions (Beginner / Scratch)** — Mean vs median vs mode skewness, variance and standard deviation, normal Gaussian bell curves, the Central Limit Theorem, and basic combinatorics.
- **Tier 2: Inferential Statistics, Hypothesis Testing & Regression Modeling (Intermediate)** — Null hypothesis significance testing (NHST), p-values and alpha thresholds, Type I and Type II errors, confidence intervals, and ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression.
- **Tier 3: Causal Inference, Bayesian Analytics & Big Data Architectures (Upper Intermediate)** — Simpson's paradox, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, Bayesian prior updating, Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) simulations, and A/B test sample sizing.
- **Tier 4: Statistical Misdirection, AI Bias & Master Data Architecture (Advanced / Masterclass)** — Darrell Huff's deceptive chart axes, survivor bias (Abraham Wald's bomber armor), algorithmic feedback loops, differential privacy, and enterprise data governance.

---

technical.requirements: Use the actual system documentation, a worked implementation and measurements. Identify inputs, outputs, constraints, tolerances, failure conditions and the limits of the example. Do not provide hazardous construction or unauthorized access procedures.
source_leads: official versioned product or standards documentation
test reports and drawings with clear provenance

science.requirements: Use original observations or experiments, an appropriate scientific reference and the actual measurement method. Distinguish mechanisms, correlations, model assumptions, uncertainty and limits of generalization.
source_leads: methods papers and current scientific reference works

handoff: Keep the BANK ID in notes. Refine the research question with an exact text edition, jurisdiction, population, product version, place, time range or clearly labeled fictional premise.
Inspect actual sources; no source was verified by generating this map. Apply the existing registry planning and idea readiness process before project creation.
Choose a current registered angle only after reading its niche-specific scope. This initial map has not checked or assigned angle plans for these entries.
Keep Q1-Q42, CAT defaults, project snapshots, output locations and production gates unchanged. Catalog counts are not production or publication counts.
Review neighboring banks for semantic overlap and follow the existing Phase 1 claim-ledger requirements. Add qualified review when required by the production contract.
prior_initial_map.coverage_limits: This initial map does not exhaust the niche, its regions, time periods, named case studies, texts, technical variants or disputed questions. It has not performed source-feasibility checks, semantic duplicate review of every pair, trend analysis, claim verification or episode production. Expand any category freely after identifying a real coverage gap; add categories where the subject requires them. Preserve existing IDs when refining wording and allocate new IDs only for genuinely new proposals.

open_coverage.next_step: Select dated jurisdictions, editions, named sites, populations or product versions for the active proposals. Inspect actual sources before making factual claims; no research or production readiness was certified.
